withheld.headline: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
withheld.evidence: Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children. Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks. But German police were already closing in on him. After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany. Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine". Both he and his country have denied any involvement. It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea. Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat. Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August. Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop. Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial. And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either. His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up. A renewed Russian campaign of strikes on power and energy infrastructure has made some contemplate leaving Ukraine's capital. Ukraine accused Russia of targeting two crowded vehicles in the front line city of Kramatorsk to kill as many civilians as possible.

As war rages inside Sudan and the humanitarian aid network nears collapse, millions of refugees both inside the country and in neighbouring nations are losing hope they will ever be able to return home safely. Instead, they fight for survival in isolated refugee camps, which are bursting at the seams. The Independent visited four Sudanese refugee camps in eastern Chad, where more than one million Sudanese refugees currently reside in isolated desert camps. Inside a 6m² shelter in the Goudrane Camp in Chad, a baby born in the battle for the city of El Fasher in western Sudan, wriggles on the carpet. Inside the tarpaulin walls, his mother, Maymauna, 27, cushions the back of her son’s head. Families also recount how they were specifically targeted and massacred by RSF soldiers, a predominantly Arab group, because they were members of the Masalit tribe, one of the largest ethnic African tribes in western Sudan before the war. Human rights investigators have since called attacks initiated by the RSF and allied Arab militias examples of ethnic cleansing, while the United Nations found ‘hallmarks of genocide’ in El Fasher. “For them, suffocation stops the slower, more painful death from thirst and starvation.” But last month, despite digging more than 128 metres deep into the Goudrane camp’s dusty ground, no water was found in the east part of the camp. “We need to create long-term solutions quickly because the need right now is so great in the camps.” Alongside warnings from the International Criminal Court (ICC) of further “mass atrocities” unfolding in El Obeid, a central Sudanese city of 500,000 people, drone attacks in the west of Sudan have been edging steadily closer to the border with Chad this year. Then, less than one week later, an air strike killed at least 12 people at a border fuel market on Thursday, according to Chadian officials. “People are living in constant insecurity and without sufficient access to water and food,” he adds. “The funding is simply not enough to support their basic, lifesaving needs as the war continues.”

withheld.headline: Seaweed Farming on a Madagascar Island Balances Livelihoods and Lagoon
withheld.evidence: On the small island of Nosy Boraha, off Madagascar's northeastern coast, an unusual agricultural boom is unfolding beneath the surface of a shallow turquoise lagoon. Farmers wade through water barely five meters deep, tying fragments of a reddish seaweed known locally as cottonii to lines anchored in the sand. The crop, Kappaphycus alvarezii, is prized worldwide as a source of carrageenan, a gelling agent that ends up in everything from ice cream to toothpaste. As wild fish stocks around the island decline, seaweed farming has emerged as a vital supplementary income for villagers such as those of Ilampy, and it has been folded into Madagascar's national blue economy strategy as a flagship of sustainable coastal development. Yet a new interdisciplinary study published in PLOS Sustainability and Transformation suggests that the story of this booming aquaculture is far more intricate than a simple success narrative, weaving together ecology, anthropology, and environmental law in a single portrait of a lagoon under change. The research, led by Isabel Urbina-Barreto of the IRD and colleagues including Rindra Razandriarison, Aline Tribollet, and a team spanning French and Malagasy institutions, set out in 2024 to answer questions that most single-discipline studies leave unasked. What does seaweed cultivation actually do to the benthic habitats of a tropical lagoon? This kind of triangulation is rare in aquaculture research, where environmental monitoring and social science often proceed on separate tracks, and it allowed the researchers to see connections that would otherwise remain invisible. Within the zones used for seaweed cultivation, the ecologists identified four genera of seagrass and three genera of macroalgae, while coral communities, made up of approximately four genera, were found mainly concentrated near the reef crest, at some distance from the main farming areas. The scale of cultivation is more modest than the headline numbers might suggest. The company Nosy Boraha Seaweed holds rights to operate across about 300 hectares of the lagoon, an area that sounds enormous until one learns that the actual cultivation plots cover only 8.3 percent of that concession. Whether that expansion proceeds without degrading the lagoon will depend on the environmental safeguards that accompany it, a question the study addresses directly. To probe those safeguards, the researchers measured nutrients in the water, comparing dissolved inorganic nitrogen and phosphate levels inside farming zones with control areas where no seaweed was grown. On the social side, the anthropological component of the study painted a picture of opportunity shadowed by hardship. A., Chauvin, A., Solofoharimanana, H., Lagoutte, E., Stoica, G., David, V., Cuet, P., Andrianaivoravelona, D., Museux, M., Jan, S., & Tribollet, A. Towards sustainable seaweed aquaculture in Nosy Boraha, Madagascar: Insights from social and ecological sciences.

withheld.headline: Hittite royal archive with 184 tablets unearthed in central Türkiye
withheld.evidence: A royal archive unearthed at the ancient Hittite settlement of Samuha, in present-day Sivas in central Türkiye, has shed new light on the Hittite Empire , revealing records of a deadly epidemic, military threats and royal life dating back about 3,400 years. Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced that archaeologists uncovered 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments during the 2026 excavations at Kayalıpınar in Sivas’ Yıldızeli district. Together with 53 tablets and fragments found at the site last year, the number of discoveries has reached 184. The documents, dating to the reign of King Tudhaliya II, are considered the most extensive Hittite-language archive discovered in the 21st century, according to the excavation team. The ancient settlement is known as Samuha in Assyrian and Hittite sources. The tablets, written in Hittite and Hurrian, provide firsthand records of state administration, military affairs, religious practices and the experiences of the royal family. “The royal archive at Kayalıpınar has taken its place in history as the most comprehensive Hittite-language archive uncovered in the 21st century,” Ersoy said in a statement shared on social media. Another tablet records her death and the funeral rites performed for her. The archive also contains evidence of the military pressures facing the Hittite state. The generals warned that the Hittite army could be destroyed if the requested reinforcements failed to arrive. The newly discovered texts also offer insight into Hittite divination practices, particularly the use of birds to interpret omens. The archive includes texts covering divination, correspondence, rituals and prayers, offering researchers new material for studying Hittite religious practices as well as the development of the Hittite language and scribal culture. The 53 cuneiform tablets and fragments discovered in 2025 are believed to have belonged to the same royal archive. The texts are dated to the reign of Tudhaliya II and are expected to provide new information on Hittite political and military history, religious practices, language and administrative culture. Excavations at Kayalıpınar have been conducted since 2021 with the permission of the Culture and Tourism Ministry under the direction of associate professor Çiğdem Maner of the Department of Archaeology and History of Art at Koç University.
